These are the playmates, or the company, or the trinkets, or the pastimes of people, and the kindness of people; these pull them here and there, and tear at their heart and their inner being, so that they must necessarily rot in all divine life and in a divine seriousness, and they do not feel God’s grace and devotion. To a person, this small temptation is often much more harmful than great trials, for a person guards against the latter with diligence and considers them wrong; but one does not wish to pay attention to these small failings, nor consider them wrong. Just as all things that one does not acknowledge are much more harmful than those one does acknowledge, so too is this danger, which one does not hold or consider of much importance, such as companionship, society, or pleasure in created things. Just as the stag is heated by every hunt, and its thirst increases all the more thereby, so should a person be heated by every temptation toward divine love for our Lord, and be incited or compelled by every trial in true thirst to run more and more into God, where one finds nothing but truth, joy, righteousness, and comfort. <note>original: *)</note>

Now, hunters sometimes do this: when the stag is too tired and too thirsty, they feed the dogs a little, and these are thus held back. When they are certain of the stag in the animal park, they let the stag walk about a little, so that it is somewhat strengthened thereby, so that it may then better endure the hunt. Our Lord does the same for the person; when He sees that the hunt is becoming too much for them, and the trial too great, He holds them back a little, and then a drop falls into the mouth of the person’s heart. To summarize everything stated thus far into a single concept, it is necessary first to remind the reader that the subject here is not the origin of experience, but rather what is contained within it. The former belongs to empirical psychology and could never be properly developed even there without the latter, which pertains to the critique of knowledge and especially of the understanding.

Experience consists of intuitions, which belong to sensibility, and of judgments, which are solely a function of the understanding. However, those judgments that the understanding makes merely from sensory intuitions are by no means yet judgments of experience. In the former case, the judgment would only connect perceptions as they are given in sensory intuition; in the latter case, however, the judgments must state what experience is in general, and consequently not what mere perception, the validity of which is merely subjective, contains. The judgment of experience must therefore, beyond sensory intuition and its logical connection (after it has been made general through comparison), add something to a judgment that determines the synthetic judgment as necessary and thereby as universally valid. The satisfaction in the good is bound up with interest.
It is not good, because although it immediately pleases the senses, it displeases when considered indirectly, that is, through the reason that looks toward the consequences. Even in the judgment of health, one can still notice this distinction. To anyone who possesses it, it is immediately agreeable (at least negatively, that is, as the removal of all physical pains). But in order to say that it is good, one must still direct it through reason toward purposes, namely that it is a state that makes us fit for all our tasks. With regard to happiness <note>a) 1st ed.: "But regarding happiness" etc.</note>, everyone ultimately believes that the greatest sum (in terms of both quantity and duration) of the enjoyments of life can be called a true, and even the highest, good. Yet reason resists even this. Enjoyment is pleasure. But if it is aimed at this alone, it would be foolish to be scrupulous regarding the means that provide it to us, whether it were obtained passively, from the generosity of nature, or through self-activity and our own actions. However, reason will never be persuaded that the existence of a person <note>b) "in itself" is missing in the 1st ed.</note> who lives merely to enjoy (and in this intention is ever so busy), even if he were to best serve others who are all equally out for enjoyment alone as a means to that end, and this because he would share in every pleasure through sympathy, has a value in itself. Only through what he does, without regard for enjoyment, in full freedom and independent of what nature might provide him passively, does he give his existence as the existence of a person an absolute <note>c) "absolute" is missing in the 1st ed.</note> value; and happiness, with all the fullness of its pleasantness, is by no means an unconditional good.*)

We also wanted to know from where they had brought that maize, and they told us from where the sun sets, and that it was found throughout that land; but the nearest place was along that path.

They told us the path was up that river toward the North, and that for seventeen days' journey we would find nothing else to eat but a fruit they call <term>chacan</term> <gloss>a type of bitter/dry fruit</gloss>, and that they mash it between stones, yet even after this effort, it can hardly be eaten because it is so rough and dry. And that was the truth, for they showed it to us there and we could not eat it. They also told us that while we traveled up the river, we would always be passing through people who were their enemies and spoke their same language, and that they had nothing to give us to eat; but that they would receive us with very good will, and would give us many cotton blankets, hides, and other things they possessed. However, it still seemed to them that we should by no means take that path.

Doubtful of what we should do, and which path we should take that would be more to our purpose and benefit, we remained with them for two days. They gave us beans and squash to eat. Their way of cooking them is so new that, for that reason, I wanted to write it down here, so that it may be seen and known how diverse and strange are the inventions and industries of human beings. They do not possess pots, and to cook what they wish, they fill a large half-gourd with water and throw into the fire many stones that they can most easily heat. They take them from the fire, and when they see they are burning hot, they pick them up with wooden tongs and drop them into the water in the gourd until they make it boil with the heat the stones carry. When they see the water boiling, they throw into it what they are to cook. Throughout this time, they do nothing but take out some stones and add others that are burning hot to keep the water boiling so as to cook what they wish, and that is how they cook.
